title: Quill shell-core bridge
description: Messages between the Swift app shell and the Rust core. JSON-RPC 2.0 notifications, one JSON object per line, over a Unix domain socket whose path the shell passes to the core in QUILL_SHELL_SOCKET. The shell listens; the core connects. The shell knows command names, never mail semantics. Every message here has an example under schema/examples that both sides test against; change all three together.

commands.list.description: Core to shell, once at startup. Every command, in the order menus should list them.

name.description: The stable name, as used in keys.toml and command.run.

keys.description: Key sequences bound to the command, preferred first, in Quill's notation: "j", "g g", "ctrl-k", "cmd-enter".

menu.description: The menu the command appears in. Absent for plain cursor movement, which has no menu item.

symbol.description: An SF Symbol name. A command with one may be shown in the toolbar.

state.update.description: Core to shell, whenever any of it changes. Always the whole state, never a delta.

context.description: Where the keyboard focus is inside the terminal UI.

enabled.description: Names of the commands that would do something right now. Menu items and toolbar buttons for every other command are disabled.

checked.description: Names of the commands that switch something on and off, and have it on right now. Their menu items are shown checked; every other command's is not.

unread.description: Unread messages across all inboxes, for the Dock badge.

background.description: The colour the terminal UI is drawn on, as #rrggbb in lower case. The shell gives it to every terminal it shows as the colour of a cell nothing has painted: the core's own, and the editor's beside it. Left out when the theme leaves the background to the terminal; the shell's terminals then keep their own colours.

foreground.description: The colour of the terminal UI's text, as #rrggbb in lower case, given to the shell's terminals as the colour of text nothing has coloured. Left out when the theme leaves it to the terminal.

appearance.description: Whether the app is to be light, dark, or as the Mac is: what the settings say. The shell's own parts go by it: with light or dark, its windows, sheets and the reading pane are that, whatever the Mac is; with system, or left out, they are as the Mac is and change with it.

pane.preview.description: Core to shell. Show files in a Quick Look pane beside the terminal: one at a time, starting with the one at `index`. The user steps through the rest with the arrow keys while the pane has the focus.

path.description: Absolute path of a file the shell can read.

index.description: Which of the items to show first, from 0. Less than the number of items.

pane.play.description: Core to shell. Play a video or audio file in a player pane beside the terminal.

path.description: Absolute path of a file the shell can read.

reading.show.description: Core to shell. Show an HTML file the core has already sanitized in the reading pane: the web view that stands in the reader's place beside the terminal while web reading is on. It takes the place of whatever the reading pane showed, stays until reading.close, and never takes the keyboard by itself. Scripts never run, nothing is loaded over the network unless `remote` is true, and links open in the user's browser, never in the pane.

path.description: Absolute path of the HTML file. Files beside it in the same folder may be loaded by it.

remote.description: The user has allowed this message to load remote content.

header.description: Lines of plain text to show above the page, outside it, where the page cannot reach: who the message is from and to, and when it was sent. Each is one line, with no control characters, of at most 2000 bytes. The shell shows them and gives them no meaning.

notice.description: Something to tell the user about the page, shown in a bar of its own between the header and the page, where the page cannot reach: that remote pictures were left out of it, say. Left out when there is nothing to say. Each action is a button beside the words; using one sends command.run with its command, as a menu item would. The shell shows the words and the buttons and gives them no meaning.

text.description: One line, with no control characters, of at most 2000 bytes.

command.description: The name of a command from commands.list.

title.description: What the button says: one line of at most 64 bytes.

reading.scroll.description: Core to shell. Scroll what the reading pane shows, as a key pressed in it would. Nothing happens when there is no reading pane.

reading.close.description: Core to shell. Take the reading pane away: web reading is off.

reading.place.description: Core to shell. Where the reading pane stands, said in the terminal's own measure: while the reading pane is beside the terminal, the terminal keeps `columns` columns and the reading pane has the rest of the window. The core works it out from window.resized, so that what it draws is as wide beside the reading pane as beside its own reader, and sends it whenever web reading is on and the number changes. The shell turns columns into points with the width of a terminal cell, and may put the divider elsewhere when the user has dragged it. It says nothing about any other pane.

columns.description: How many columns the terminal keeps.

editor.place.description: Core to shell. Where the editor of pane.editor goes, and whether it has the keys. The editor runs in a terminal of its own that the shell lays over the core's terminal, exactly over the cells `place` names: where the text of the message being written would be drawn, under the fields the core still draws. Cells are counted from the top left of the terminal's screen, from 0. `covered` is how many of the place's rows, from its top, the core has drawn something over (the people offered under an address being typed): the shell does not show those rows of the editor, and does not make the editor smaller for them. With no `place` the editor is not on show, because something of the core's is drawn where it would be, and goes on running. `keys` is whether what is typed goes to the editor; otherwise it goes to the core's terminal. An editor that is not on show never has the keys. Sent whenever any of it changes; the shell keeps the last, for an editor that has yet to start, and decides nothing itself.

thumbnail.make.description: Core to shell. Make a PNG thumbnail of a file (a picture the core cannot decode, the first page of a PDF, the poster frame of a video) and write it to `out`. Answered by thumbnail.made with the same id.

path.description: Absolute path of the file to picture.

out.description: Absolute path to write the PNG to.

size.description: The longest side wanted, in pixels.

file.open.description: Core to shell. Open a file in the application the user's Mac opens its kind with. Only ever on an explicit key press by the user.

path.description: Absolute path of a file the shell can read.

files.save.description: Core to shell. Ask the user where to save a copy of a file, with the native save panel, and save it there. Answered by files.saved.

path.description: Absolute path of the file to copy.

name.description: The name to offer in the panel.

link.open.description: Core to shell. Open a web or mail address in the user's default browser or mail program. The shell opens nothing else: no other scheme, and nothing outside printable ASCII.

url.description: An http, https or mailto address.

pane.close.description: Core to shell. While an editor started by pane.editor is running: ask it to save what has been written and leave, in its own keys, as someone at the keyboard would; editor.exited follows. Otherwise: close the second pane and return focus to the terminal.

files.pick.description: Core to shell. Ask the user to choose files with the native open panel. What they choose arrives as files.dropped; cancelling sends nothing.

clipboard.write.description: Core to shell. Put text on the system clipboard: the user copied or cut it in the terminal UI.

files.dropped.description: Shell to core. The user chose files in the open panel or dropped them onto the window. The shell does not know what they are for; the core decides.

paths.description: Absolute paths of files the core can read.

temporary.description: The files are copies the shell made for the core, which removes each once it has read it. False: they are the user's own files and are left alone.

command.run.description: Shell to core. A menu item or toolbar button was used.

thumbnail.made.description: Shell to core. The answer to thumbnail.make: the PNG was written to the path asked for, or could not be made.

files.saved.description: Shell to core. The answer to files.save: the copy was saved, or the user cancelled or it could not be written.

name.description: The name the file was saved under, or was offered under if it was not saved.

notify.post.description: Core to shell. Show a notification, in place of any earlier one with the same id. The shell shows the words as plain text and returns the id, and an action's name, in notify.used. It knows nothing else about them.

id.description: The core's name for the notification.

actions.description: Buttons on the notification, in order. None is allowed.

foreground.description: Using this action brings Quill's window forward: what it starts needs the user there, as a reply does. Left out, the action is done in the background.

notify.clear.description: Core to shell. Take down the notifications with these ids, shown or waiting. One that is not there is not an error.

notify.used.description: Shell to core. The user clicked a notification, or one of its actions.

action.description: The name of the action chosen. Left out when the notification itself was clicked.

url.open.description: Shell to core. The Mac asked Quill to open a mail address: a mailto link clicked in another application. Only mailto addresses are passed on.

spell.check.description: Core to shell. Check the spelling of some text with the system's checker, in the user's languages. Answered by spell.checked with the same id. Nothing is learned or remembered from the text.

spell.checked.description: Shell to core. The answer to spell.check: where the misspelt words are, each as the byte offsets of its start and end in the text as UTF-8, in order and not overlapping.

spell.suggest.description: Core to shell. Ask the system's checker what a misspelt word might have been meant to be. Answered by spell.suggested with the same id.

spell.suggested.description: Shell to core. The answer to spell.suggest: words to offer, the likeliest first. None is an answer too.

pane.editor.description: Core to shell. Run an editor on a draft, in a terminal of its own that is laid over the core's where editor.place says. The draft is the text of the message alone: the fields above it are still the core's, drawn in its own terminal. `argv` is the whole command: the program by its absolute path, then its arguments, the draft file last. The core makes it, exactly as it does for an editor that takes the terminal Quill itself is in: the program is the user's own (the one their settings name, or the one of the editor's name found on the PATH), and it reads the user's own settings for it. The shell runs that argv as it is, never through a shell, in `dir`, in the environment the app has, with QUILL_DRAFT_DIR set to `dir`. `dir` is the draft's own folder, where the editor and the core leave each other notes. `editor` says what kind of editor it is, which is how the shell asks it to save and leave when pane.close arrives: `vim` (also anything that takes Vim's keys), `nano` (also Pico) or `mg`. `title` is what the message is called, for the shell to name the editor by where it names it at all. Answered by editor.exited when the editor ends, or at once if it could not be started.

argv.description: The program, by its absolute path, and then its arguments.

editor.exited.description: Shell to core. The answer to pane.editor. `ran` is false when the editor could not be started (the one asked for is not there); `status` is then 0. Otherwise `status` is what it exited with: 0 for a normal exit, anything else for Vim's :cq or a crash.

form.show.description: Core to shell. Show a form in a sheet on the main window, in place of whatever form the sheet shows now: the sheet is opened if it is not up, and a sheet that is up is given the new form where it stands, whatever question the last one asked. A form is anything the core asks before going on: the steps of adding an account, a sign-in to wait for, a certificate to accept, a time to name, a thing to confirm. The core sends the whole form again whenever any of it changes, and the shell shows exactly the fields it names, in order. The shell lays the form out and knows nothing of what it is for; it keeps what the user has typed in a field unless the step is another one or the core's value for the field has changed. A secret field never has a value: the core does not send one back. What the user does arrives as form.used.

step.description: Which step of which form this is: a name no other question on show at the same time shares. Sent back in form.used.

error.description: What is wrong, said below the fields.

busy.description: What is being waited for, in words: an answer from a server, or the user doing something elsewhere (signing in, in the browser). The shell says it beside a progress indicator. While it is there the fields take no typing; which buttons can be pressed is said by each button.

fields.description: The fields, in order. Each has a name of its own, and at most one has the focus. A sheet asks and waits for a button, so it has none of the kinds that say what the user did as they do it (toggle, number, list, button): those are the settings window's.

buttons.description: The buttons, from left to right. Each has a name of its own; at most one is pressed by return and at most one by esc.

role.description: The key that presses it: return for `default`, esc for `cancel`. Left out for a button no key presses.

formId.description: The name of a step, field, option or button of a form.

formField.description: One field of a form, or of a pane of the settings window. `focus` says where the keyboard starts; `help` is said under the field in small print. The shell knows a field by its kind and never by what it is for.

oneOf.description: A line of text to type.
A line of text that is not shown as it is typed: a password. It has no value: the core never sends one.
One of a few options. `value` is the name of the one chosen, and is one of them.

Text shown to be read off, selected or copied, and typed somewhere else: a code to sign in with, the page to type it at. The shell shows it large, in a fixed-width face, and it can be selected. It is only shown, so it never has the focus. Neither side prints its value or writes it to a log or a dump.
Something that is on or off: a checkbox. `label` stands beside it as any field's does and may be empty; `title` is the checkbox's own words.

A number from `min` to `max`, both included; with no `max` there is no most. `value` is within them. It is shown with at most `decimals` places after the point and stepped by `step`, which is more than nothing. `unit` is said after it.

Rows to look down and pick one of, and things to do, as buttons under them. An action with `row` true is done to the row picked, and can be pressed only while a row that names it in its own `actions` is picked; one with `row` false needs no row. `empty` is said in the rows' place when there are none. Which row is picked is the shell's to keep.

detail.description: Said under the title, in small print.

actions.description: The names of the list's actions that can be asked of this row.

oneOf.description: Something to press, that starts something: a button. `label` stands beside it as any field's does and may be empty; `title` is on the button. A press comes back in settings.used as the action `press`, with no row. Only the settings window has one: a sheet has buttons of its own.

form.close.description: Core to shell. Take the sheet down: the form is over. Nothing the user typed in it is kept. With no sheet up it does nothing.

form.used.description: Shell to core. The user pressed a button of the form in the sheet, or changed one of its choices. `values` is what its text fields and choices held at that moment, by field name (a choice by the name of its option); `secrets` is the same for its secret fields, kept apart so that neither side ever prints them. The button esc presses (role `cancel`) sends neither: both objects are empty. A changed choice sends the values and no secrets. The shell does not keep a secret once it has sent it, and neither side writes one to a log or a dump. The shell does not close the sheet itself: the core answers with form.show or form.close.

step.description: The step the form was at, as form.show named it. The core drops an answer about a step the form has left.

button.description: The name of the button pressed. Left out when a choice was changed and no button pressed: the values are sent so that the form can change with it.

window.resized.description: Shell to core. How many columns the terminal would have if it had the whole window to itself: what the window has room for, whatever stands beside the terminal now. Sent once the terminal's cell size is known and whenever the number changes. The core lays out by it while a pane of the shell's stands in the reader's place, and answers with reading.place.

settings.show.description: Core to shell. What the settings window shows: its panes in order, each with the settings it holds as they stand now. Sent in answer to settings.opened, again after every settings.used (whether or not the change was made, so that the window always ends up showing what is so), and whenever any of it changes while the window is open. The shell lays the panes out as a settings window with a toolbar of them, keeps which pane the user last had, and knows nothing of what any setting means. With no panes the settings cannot be shown or changed from here (the settings file has a mistake in it): `problem` says what, and the window says it and offers to open the file. With panes, `problem` is why the last change was not made.

panes.description: The panes, in the order of their toolbar buttons. Each has a name of its own.

title.description: On the pane's toolbar button, and the window's title while the pane is on show.

symbol.description: The name of the SF Symbol on the pane's toolbar button.

fields.description: The settings, in order, each with a name of its own in its pane. A setting has no button to wait for: what the user does with one arrives at once as settings.used. Settings have no secret and no code, and no field has the focus: the keyboard is the user's to put.

more.description: Said at the foot of the pane, beside a button of the shell's own that opens the settings file: what more can be set there.

settings.opened.description: Shell to core. The user opened the settings window, or brought it forward. The core reads the settings afresh and answers with settings.show.

settings.closed.description: Shell to core. The settings window was closed: nothing more need be sent for it.

settings.used.description: Shell to core. The user did something in the settings window: gave a field another value (`value`: true or false for a toggle, a number for a number, text for a text field, the name of the option for a choice), or asked for one of a list's actions (`action`, with `row` the name of the row picked when the action is done to a row), or pressed a button (`action` is `press`, with no row). A value or an action, never both. The core checks it against what it described, makes the change or does not, and answers with settings.show either way.

themes.pick.description: Core to shell. Ask the user to choose a theme to import, with the shell's own chooser: the themes of a Ghostty installed on this Mac, or a file from anywhere. The shell copies the one chosen into the themes folder beside the settings file and says so with themes.imported; cancelling sends nothing. The shell reads a theme file only to show its colours in the chooser: what a theme is, and whether a file is one, is the core's to say.

appearance.changed.description: Shell to core. Whether the Mac is in its dark appearance: sent once as the shell starts and whenever the Mac changes. The core goes by it while the settings say the appearance is the system's, and draws with its dark or its light theme accordingly.

themes.imported.description: Shell to core. A theme file was put in the themes folder beside the settings file, under this name: the user chose it in the shell's chooser. The core reads the folder again, and if the file is a theme it can use, makes it the theme in force and says so with settings.show. A name is the name of a file in that folder and nothing else: no path separator or colon, no control character, no dot to start with, no space at either end, not ending in .toml, at most 100 bytes.

keys.list.description: Core to shell, at startup and again whenever the keys change. Every key Quill has, under headings and in the order to show them: what the list drawn in the terminal has. The shell keeps the latest for its window of keys, which keys.show brings up, and draws a window that is open again. It shows what it is given and works nothing out.

keys.description: The key sequences bound to it, preferred first, in Quill's notation. Empty for a command no key is bound to.

keys.show.description: Core to shell. Bring up the window of keys, showing the latest keys.list: the user asked for the list of every key from a menu. The window is not modal and stays up beside the mail until the user closes it. Asked for by its key, the list is drawn in the terminal instead and this is not sent.

app.will_quit.description: Shell to core. The app is quitting: flush and exit cleanly.
